turns.prompt_text: I have two Lego gears here with me hooked up to each other. each one has 24 teeth, if I hold one in place and move the other one concentric around it, I can get a full rotation when I only move half of the other gear
turns.response_html:
That is a classic mechanical observation that often feels like a "glitch" in physics until you break down the frame of reference. You are experiencing the 2n+1 principle of planetary gears.

Why it happens

When you mesh two gears of equal size (let's call them Gear A and Gear B) in a fixed-axis setup—like they are pinned to a board—turning Gear A once causes Gear B to turn once in the opposite direction.

However, when you hold Gear A still and orbit Gear B around it, Gear B is subject to two different rotations simultaneously:

  1. The Mesh Rotation: As Gear B travels around the circumference of Gear A, the teeth force it to rotate on its own axis. Since they have the same number of teeth ($24:24$), one full orbit should equal one rotation.
  2. The Orbital Rotation: Simply by completing a $360^{\circ}$ circle around Gear A, Gear B has completed one rotation relative to the room, regardless of teeth.

When you add these together, Gear B completes two full rotations for every one orbit around Gear A.

The "Halfway" Mark

Because Gear B rotates twice as fast as it orbits, moving it only halfway ($180^{\circ}$) around the fixed gear causes Gear B to complete one full $360^{\circ}$ rotation on its own axis.

Fun Fact: The Coin Paradox

This isn't unique to gears; it's often called the Coin Rotation Paradox. If you take two identical quarters, hold one still, and roll the other around its edge without slipping, the moving quarter will have performed two full rotations by the time it gets back to the start.

If you want to try something even weirder with your Legos:

  • Try orbiting a small gear around a large fixed gear.
  • The formula for the number of rotations Gear B makes is $1 + (\frac{T_a}{T_b})$, where $T$ is the number of teeth.
  • In your case: $1 + (\frac{24}{24}) = 2$ rotations per orbit.

turns.prompt_text: The part I don't understand is that if they both have 24 teeth and how is one making a full rotation while it only moves around half of the other
turns.response_html:
It definitely feels like the math shouldn't add up! The trick is that Gear B is actually rotating around two different points at the same time.

To visualize why it completes a full rotation at the halfway mark, imagine a single tooth on the moving gear (Gear B) starts at the "12 o'clock" position.

1. The "Rolling" Motion (Relative to the Gear)

Since both gears have 24 teeth, if you roll Gear B halfway around Gear A, it has touched 12 teeth on Gear A. To do that, Gear B must have also clicked through 12 of its own teeth.

  • Clicking through 12 out of 24 teeth is a half-rotation ($180^{\circ}$) relative to the point where the gears touch.

2. The "Orbit" Motion (Relative to the Room)

While Gear B is clicking through those 12 teeth, it is also physically moving through space to the opposite side of Gear A.

  • By reaching the halfway point, the entire gear has traveled $180^{\circ}$ around the circle.

Adding them together

When you combine these two motions, the "half-turn" from the teeth and the "half-turn" from the orbit happen in the same direction.

  • $180^{\circ}$ (Teeth) + $180^{\circ}$ (Orbit) = $360^{\circ}$ (One Full Rotation)

By the time you are halfway around, the tooth that started at the top has "rolled" to the bottom of its own axis, but the "orbit" has carried that bottom back up to the top position relative to your ceiling.

A simple way to see it:

If you had a "magic" gear with zero teeth that didn't spin at all, and you just moved it halfway around the fixed gear, it would look upside down to you (a half-turn). Because your Lego gears do have teeth, they have to "roll" on top of that movement, which provides the extra half-turn needed to finish the rotation early!
